title: Newton's law of universal gravitation
log: 2026-10-27T00:53:13Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

draft.title: Newton's law of universal gravitation
card: Every two masses attract each other. The forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, whatever the masses are.
The size of the force is F = GMm/r². M and m are the two masses in kg, r is the distance between their centres in metres, and G is the universal gravitational constant.
F is proportional to each mass. Doubling one mass doubles F.
F is inversely proportional to r². Doubling the distance cuts F to one quarter, and halving the distance makes F four times larger.
draft.remember: Force grows with both masses and falls with the square of the distance between centres.

a.q: The distance between the centres of two masses is tripled. The masses stay the same. What happens to the gravitational force between them?
opts: It becomes one ninth of its original size
It becomes one third of its original size
It becomes three times its original size
It becomes nine times its original size
a.why: F is proportional to 1/r², so tripling r divides F by 3², which is 9. One third is tempting, but it treats the force as inversely proportional to r rather than to r².
a.clue: The distance is squared in the formula.

b.q: A 2000 kg probe is near a moon. The moon pulls on the probe with a force of 800 N. What is the force the probe exerts on the moon?
opts: 800 N, directed away from the probe
Far less than 800 N, as the probe has less mass
Far more than 800 N, as the moon has more mass
b.why: The two forces are an equal and opposite pair, so the probe pulls on the moon with 800 N towards the probe. The moon's larger mass does not make its pull on the probe larger than the probe's pull on it. It only means the moon's acceleration is far smaller.
b.clue: The card says the two forces are equal in size.

a.best: It becomes one ninth of its original size
